A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORBIT framework and retain matched core experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original ORBIT training results on HealthBench and InfoBench, component ablations, distributional analyses and a consultation case study.

after.justification: v4 retains original HealthBench experiments and adds judge comparisons, physician annotations, seed-source experiments and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: The default retrieval, rubric rewards, GRPO, filtering and staged-restart procedure remains substantially unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds an optional synthetic seed-construction approach using multiple LLM generators, summarization and contrastive filtering. This is a limited procedural extension; the newly supplied pseudocode mainly documents the existing pipeline.

E1.justification: v4 removes v2 Section 4.5's InfoBench-Hard evaluation and associated WildChat training samples, eliminating the demonstrated non-medical instruction-following domain. The medical dialogue sources and HealthBench coverage remain; the expanded DoctorAgent-RL/MTMedDialog description clarifies retained data provenance.

E2.justification: v4 adds standalone Baichuan-M2-distilled SFT comparisons, no-retrieval and synthetic-seed alternatives, and training-judge variants (Tables 6, 9 and 16). It removes GPT-OSS-120B (high) as a Table 1 contestant and DeepSeek-R1/V3 judges from the calibration comparison formerly in v2 Table 3. The original rubric-generator comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New designs include fixed-response judging on 200 training-pool cases, blinded physician review of 60 cases, matched 200-case HealthBench comparisons, and seed/judge experiments with specified 140/200-step budgets. Existing HealthBench decoding settings remain unchanged (v2 Table 6; v4 Table 15). Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filtering, scaling, generator and SFT ablations, v4 adds training-judge sensitivity, physician validation, seed-source controls, within/across-case rubric redundancy, prompt-level contamination diagnostics, reward/entropy trajectories and stringent-filter failure analysis. Appendix G adds three scored clinical cases while retaining the original consultation example.

E5.justification: v2 provides point estimates and identifies single-seed scaling runs. v4 adds bootstrap confidence intervals for judge agreement, 1,000-resample paired confidence intervals and one-sided tests on 200 benchmark cases, and three grading trials reporting mean 27.4 and standard deviation 0.42. These additions concern evaluation uncertainty; single-seed scaling experiments remain explicitly identified.

E6.justification: The headline ORBIT scores of 27.5, 33.6 and 37.3 remain unchanged. v4 adds substantial findings, including 90.7% physician-rated rubric meaningfulness, seed-source scores of 17.89 versus 10.69, and a matched-subset ORBIT–base difference of 11.05. It removes InfoBench's 42.0-to-82.9 result and numerous nonduplicated theme/axis entries when compressing appendix tables.

T1.justification: Appendix H.2 introduces mathematical definitions for prompt/rubric nearest-neighbor similarities, thresholded and joint contamination rates, and within-set redundancy (Equations 6–10). These are limited analytical additions. The core optimization mathematics is substantially retained, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: v4 removes the demonstrated beyond-medicine generality contribution and narrows performance claims to comparable-size open-source models or evaluated baselines. Its introduction instead foregrounds a contribution about learning case-conditioned clinical criteria rather than evaluator preferences or reusable templates. The central 7.0-to-27.5 medical performance claim remains.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of judge quality, rubric specificity, safety–verbosity trade-offs, filtering/SFT failure mechanisms and clinical oversight requirements. Appendix H.2 qualifies generalization as unseen prompts within a shared rubric framework, tempering v2's strong t-SNE-based contamination assurances. Appendix F.7 explicitly acknowledges inconclusive superiority over distilled SFT.

D1.justification: v4 supplies retrieval model identities and retrieval counts, detailed RL/SFT hyperparameters, software and server configurations, preprocessing limits and evaluation timing (Appendices A.3 and F). These largely document retained experiments. It also replaces the abstract's repository link with a project-page link and refers to released per-case scores and a harness; their availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

R1.justification: New Appendix J substantially expands positioning against process rewards, rubric/checklist alignment and medical models, emphasizing final-response supervision, retrieved case specificity and multi-turn medical alignment. Citations also change, including adding RewardBench and Sharma et al.'s human–AI collaboration work and removing InfoBench. DoctorAgent-RL's updated title represents the same cited work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and extensive explanatory passages are rewritten, with the narrative refocused on medical validation. Limitations are integrated into the conclusion, and Appendix F is reorganized into dedicated data, baseline, training, stability, evaluation, statistics and ablation subsections. Separate failure-mode and extended-related-work sections further restructure the document.

P2.justification: v4 adds a motivation illustration, evaluator/physician panels, rubric-diversity and cost plots, training traces, heatmaps and contamination diagnostics. Several wide appendix result matrices become compact summary tables, alongside new configuration, statistical and case-study tables. Existing pipeline, radar, rollout-distribution and t-SNE figures are retained with relocation, caption editing or resizing.

improvement.justification: v2 offered sparse training/retrieval specifications and limited evidence for evaluator reliability and contamination control. v4 substantially improves auditability through detailed configurations, physician reference judgments, controlled seed/judge experiments, uncertainty estimates and prompt-level contamination diagnostics. Its explicit acknowledgment that the ORBIT–SFT confidence interval includes zero improves interpretive discipline. Removing InfoBench and detailed appendix breakdowns reduces breadth, but the gains address central reproducibility and validation weaknesses of the retained medical contribution.
